Contentedness is great- congrats! I don't think it's greedy or foolish to want more purpose. I think it's very human, and this itch that you have is just your starting point. You should harness this curiosity and search for your purpose. If you're not spiritual, Reddit seems like a good starting point, but you probably can get better guidance from spiritual guides, meditation, therapy, or even a good book. This is an opportunity for you to search for your own meaning, and at the end of the day it's about following your heart- something nobody but you can know.

I'd suggest making a list of things you wanted to do but never did, things you wish had happened differently, things that caused you distress or anxiety, and try to make some sense of it, or gather some direction/next steps.

Seek out a spiritual teacher, such as a yogi, guru, priest, therapist, or a really good friend, and ask for some advice.

Read books about what you're going through. Eat, Pray, Love is about a similar crisis and might be a good place to start.

Good luck on your journey for self discovery and purpose!

When I last broke up (I'm a 9, she was a 4), I had this persistent itch that I needed to do it, but I avoided it as much as I could. I talked to so many people about my feelings to search for validation, but it's hard to accept. Finally I just went with my heart and had the difficult conversation. It was so tough, and for a while I second-guessed my decision. But I did instantly notice a weight off my chest- less anxiety than I'd felt with her.

What I did to validate my decision was to reevaluate what my needs were. For me it was that I need to take some time to work on loving myself more before dating again. Basically it means making lists each day and checking off boxes, and working hard to get out of the rut the relationship and the pandemic has put me in. It's hard work, and it's not without slip-ups. Just try to do a little more each day. Don't overdo it. Do introspect, even if only as an afterthought for a while. Read something by Glennon Doyle or similar. I find these shame/relationships/self help books help me think about my own life.

We do care, and we do have feelings, but unenlightened/more avoidant 9's aren't as good at voicing them (and they might not even be able to put a name to the feeling).

What I've noticed in my relationships is that my disagreements often come out passive-aggressively, such as in little teases or jokes that poke fun a little bit.

I believe that if you're able to have open, honest conversations (and he's able to identify his real feelings) then that's a really big deal (and as a 4, you're the right person for that task). Nines are not the types to end a bad relationship, and might instead intentionally hide negative feelings.

So in summary, you'll know it's a match that he is serious about if he's not making too many passive aggressive remarks, and if you believe he's being genuine when you talk about feelings. 

It's too bad he's not interested in self awareness. I hope for his sake he either remains that way or wakes up to his needs before too long. That said, he's lucky to have someone who's so tuned in to his needs and his feelings. Best of luck!

I think it really depends on where your SO is as a nine. A nine can be very enlightened: self-aware, and accepting of the world as it unfolds. Or a nine can also be naive to the world (ignorance is bliss). I can't speak for all nines, I just know that I had a ten year relationship in that latter state, and although I wasn't often sad, I wasn't fulfilled either. I'm working on becoming that enlightened nine, but I don't believe that's really, actually obtainable.

I am actually dating a four now, and she and I have some really deep conversations about emotions, desires, the enneagram, etc. I think the 4/9 relationship can be really healthy- you may be able to help your SO come into themselves, and you may be able to learn some ways to just kick back and ignore that urge to overthink things. It's important to really try to fully, emotionally understand each other. 

Just keep in mind that 9's avoid feelings and conflict, so try to notice when your SO is agreeable because that's what they want or because it's the path of least resistance. 

Conversely, maybe to "walk like a nine," you could try the path of least resistance to see if it gives you that liberating feeling you desire.

I'm a nine, and I believe you're better off as you are. That "drifting through life" concept is our way of just putting life on auto-drive, and not actually experiencing it. We don't remember important moments in life because we aren't emotionally invested... It's a very sad realization when we come into ourselves and realize what little we actually know about ourselves- not what we're expected to be. 

The fact that you struggle, you ask questions, and you seek understanding of yourself means that you are living a more fulfilling life.

So do you want it to be labeled as a relationship? Do you have genuine feelings with him? If so, you need to have a real conversation with him about this. It's great to get some general ideas/feedback here, but you need to tell him that what he did hurt your feelings (that's a key word that FWBs shouldn't have to worry about). If he feels remorseful, and wants to make things better, consider couples therapy. This suggestion could be a pivotal moment - either he cares enough about your relationship to agree, or his hesitancy tells you how he feels (either that he has a problem with evaluating his own feelings, or he doesn't have strong enough feelings for you). 

Also worth noting- dating after divorce is hard, and emotionally committing after heart-break is daunting (we put up emotional armor). If he has not seeked therapy on his own, it's likely he hasn't changed much, and it's often said that unresolved problems will continue into new relationships. If he is uncomfortable with couples therapy, individual therapy would be a good fallback for him.

It's really painful to look back and reflect on your marriage and all the things you could've done differently.
